weeks.plan_title: Project 35: Document Extraction Pipeline with Validation
weeks.theme: Project 35: extract invoice fields, validate them, measure accuracy
weeks.goal: Build and evaluate a pipeline that turns invoice text into schema-validated JSON, with measured field accuracy and a human-review route.

lessons.title: Project 35 step 1: problem, schema and gold labels
lessons.build: Project #35. Write a 5-line problem statement. Fix the schema: vendor, invoice_no, date, total (Project Lab 16.3). Write 30 short invoice texts yourself; hand-label gold JSON for 10 of them as your test set and lock them. Decide the scores: per-field accuracy and all-fields-correct per document.
lessons.ask: Why must the gold labels be written before you look at any model output?
lessons.learn: Read genai Chapter 16, section 16.3 (OCR text in, validated JSON out) and Chapter 12, section 12.2 (OCR, OCR-free models, structured extraction).

lessons.title: Step 2: a rule-based first version
lessons.build: Write extract_rules(text) with regexes for the four fields and run it on your 10 gold documents. Print per-field accuracy. Handle the OCR trap of 16.4: the string $1O5.5O has letter O instead of zero; write fix_amount and test it. Save the run with a date and the git commit.
lessons.ask: Which field was hardest for rules, and what in the text made it hard?
lessons.learn: Read 16.3 again for the pipeline and the repair() idea. Skim 16.4 on OCR digit confusion and the five debugging problems.

lessons.title: Step 3: validation, repair and tests
lessons.build: Write validate(obj): required keys, types, ISO date, total as a number, and money compared with Decimal, never floats (0.10 + 0.20 is not 0.30). Add repair() for fixable errors (a total as '1,234.50'). Write 5 tests: 3 bad objects rejected, 2 repairs accepted.
lessons.ask: Which errors should repair() fix quietly, and which must go to a human?
lessons.learn: Read 12.8: exact money checks, field accuracy compounding (0.97^4 = 88.5% for four fields), confidence routing, and page token cost.

lessons.title: Step 4: add the LLM and compare
lessons.build: Write extract_llm(text) with a prompt that returns only JSON. Use any LLM API you can access, or the mock from the chapter. Parse safely, retry once with the validation error, then fall back to the rules. Score both extractors on the same 10 gold documents and log tokens per document.
lessons.ask: If the LLM returns invalid JSON 1 time in 10, what does one retry do to the failure rate?
lessons.learn: Read 12.2: when OCR plus an LLM beats OCR-free models, structured extraction prompts, schema checks, and routing failed pages to people.

lessons.title: Step 5: error analysis and the human-review route
lessons.build: Make an error table: document, field, expected, got, cause. Mark the 5 worst failures. Add confidence routing: auto-accept only if validation passes and both extractors agree; else human review. Report the straight-through rate and accuracy of the accepted set. Problem 12.2.2: 2,000 failed pages x 3 min = 100 hours.
lessons.ask: What share of documents go straight through, and how accurate is that group?
lessons.learn: Re-read the Common mistake boxes in 12.8 and the rubric in 16.4. Note which acceptance criteria your project can state as numbers.

weeks.goal: Serve a validated model, measure what batching buys, avoid unsafe formats, and size replicas and GPUs on paper.

lessons.title: A prediction service with validation and health checks
lessons.build: Build the 7.1 service: a pydantic-validated request, a /health route and a /predict route, with counters for requests, errors and latency. Practice 1: 4,850 of 5,000 answered 200 and the rest 422, so the error rate is 3%. Send a request with the key misspelt and read the status code.
lessons.ask: Why return a clear 422 for bad input instead of letting the model crash?
lessons.learn: Read 7.1: request schemas, status codes, health and readiness checks, metrics (error rate, average latency), and failing safely.

lessons.title: Batching: why one row at a time wastes time
lessons.build: Time model.predict on 1,000 single rows versus one batch of 1,000. Fit fixed cost and per-row cost from two batch sizes (Problem 7.2.1). Practice 3: 5 ms fixed + 0.02 ms per row gives 199 rows/s at batch 1 and 14,286 rows/s at batch 100.
lessons.ask: What is the price of batching in latency, and who pays it?
lessons.learn: Read 7.2: fixed versus per-row cost, micro-batching, the latency-throughput trade-off, and the p95 target of Problem 7.2.2.

lessons.title: Model formats and the pickle risk
lessons.build: Show why unpickling untrusted files is dangerous: a class whose __reduce__ prints a message when loaded (harmless demo only). Then export a logistic regression to JSON coefficients, rebuild predict in NumPy and match scikit-learn to 1e-9 (Problem 7.3.1: verify 0.5343 by hand).
lessons.ask: Why is loading a model file from the internet like running a stranger's program?
lessons.learn: Read 7.3: pickle and joblib risks, safer formats (ONNX, plain weights), version coupling, and checking a converted model against the original.

lessons.title: Serving frameworks and replica sizing
lessons.build: Problem 7.4.1: one replica serves 120 requests per second, peak is 500, and no replica may exceed 70% load. Each replica carries 84, so you need 6. Write replicas_needed(peak, per_replica, max_util) with tests. Compare two ways to serve one model: a plain function, and a framework route.
lessons.ask: Why leave 30% headroom on every replica?
lessons.learn: Read 7.4: serving frameworks, when a model server beats a plain API, and the concepts behind LLM serving (batching, KV cache, streaming).

lessons.title: Latency budgets, queues and LLM memory
lessons.build: Problem 7.5.2: 250 requests per second x 0.08 s means 20 busy worker slots. Draw the 300 ms p99 budget of Problem 7.5.1 as a table. Then LLM memory: kv_per_token = 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 131,072, so 4,096 tokens take 0.54 GB (Problem 7.6.1). Size Problem 7.6.2.
lessons.ask: At 90% utilisation, why does p99 latency blow up even though the average looks fine?
lessons.learn: Read 7.5 (latency budgets, queues, autoscaling delays) and 7.6 (KV cache per token, bandwidth bound for decoding, batching users).

weeks.theme: Deployment strategies: shadow, canary, A/B, bandits, release maths
weeks.goal: Choose and simulate a release strategy, and check a rollout with the right statistics (SRM, paired tests, sequential canaries).

lessons.title: Shadow, blue/green and rollback
lessons.build: Simulate a shadow run: score 5,000 requests with an old and a new model, count different decisions (Problem 8.1.1) and decide what you would check next. Implement blue/green as a one-line pointer switch and a rollback that restores it, with a test.
lessons.ask: Why does a shadow deployment never show the new model's answer to users?
lessons.learn: Read 8.1: shadow, blue/green, what a rollback needs (old version still warm), and what to compare in shadow mode.

lessons.title: Canary releases with automatic rollback
lessons.build: Simulate a canary with a true 2.0% error rate and a 3.5% limit, at 100, 500 and 2,000 requests, 10,000 trials each. Print how often a good model is rolled back. Practice 1: 40 errors in 2,000 is 2.0%, so pass. Explain the trend of Problem 8.2.1.
lessons.ask: Why does a good model get rolled back more often when the canary sample is small?
lessons.learn: Read 8.2: canary stages, error limits, minimum sample size, automatic rollback, and the false-alarm table.

lessons.title: A/B tests of models: sample size and power
lessons.build: Problem 8.3.1: 3,841 per arm for 10% to 12%, the same number as in week 112. Simulate 2,000 tests with true rates 10% and 12% and 3,841 per arm; the share with p below 0.05 should be near 80%. Check the z value of Problem 8.3.2.
lessons.ask: Why is a 0.5-point difference with 500 users per group (Practice 3) not trustworthy?
lessons.learn: Read 8.3: randomising users, metrics and guardrails, sample size, running whole cycles, and not peeking.

lessons.title: Bandits and choosing a strategy
lessons.build: Simulate 10,000 users and two models with conversion 10% and 12%. Compare a fixed 50/50 split, Thompson sampling and an oracle that always picks the better one (Problem 8.4.1). Then Problem 8.4.2: write which strategy you would use at each stage of a fraud-model release.
lessons.ask: When is a bandit a bad choice compared with a fixed A/B test?
lessons.learn: Read 8.4: epsilon-greedy and Thompson sampling, regret, and a table of which strategy fits which risk and speed.

lessons.build: Problem 8.5.1: a planned 90/10 split gave 9,700 and 800 requests, expected 9,450 and 1,050; chi-square is 66, so the split is broken (week 112's SRM). Problem 8.5.2: the new model won 91 of 149 disagreements; compute the paired z, about 2.7. Run the SPRT of 8.5.3.

lessons.learn: Read 8.5: split checks, paired tests on the same requests, sequential canaries, and the guardrail example of Problem 8.5.5.
